narrative:
The model estimated a 56.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above a 50% failure threshold, your application was denied. This does not mean failure is certain; it means the model judged the risk high enough to reject admission at this time. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The denial was driven by three factors in ranked order. Your LSAT score was the most influential factor overall, and it actually weighed toward passing in the model’s assessment, even though your score of 36 was slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37.18. The second most important factor was your third-year class decile. Your decile of 2, compared with an accepted-student average near 5.79, pushed the prediction toward bar failure. The third factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.50, compared with an accepted-student average of 3.23, it also pushed toward failure. Together, the third-year rank and GPA concerns outweighed the favorable LSAT signal, producing a failure probability above the denial cutoff.

To improve your next application, focus on the areas that drove the decision: strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a graduate program, and seek advising on how to explain or address your third-year rank and GPA. You may also consider targeted bar-readiness preparation and reapplying after showing sustained academic improvement.
